analysis.one_liner: Stops employers from automatically moving retirees into Medicare Advantage without their signed-up consent.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill to require retirees to opt in before being enrolled in employer Medicare Advantage plans was referred to two House committees and its Health subcommittee but never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some employers switch retired workers and their spouses from traditional Medicare into private Medicare Advantage plans automatically, without asking them. This bill would require each person to affirmatively choose to move, with silence meaning they stay in traditional Medicare and the employer keeps paying for that coverage. It also states the sense of Congress that seniors have a right to choose between traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and older workers whose employers offer a private Medicare Advantage plan. They keep the choice between traditional Medicare and a private plan, and no one is moved into the private plan just because they missed a letter or failed to return a form. People who did not respond to an enrollment ask stay in traditional Medicare, with the employer required to keep paying for that coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits public and private employers from involuntarily forcing seniors to shift from Medicare to Medicare Advantage.

Requires employers to offer an opt-in choice to move from traditional Medicare to Medicare Advantage, and treats a failure to respond to that ask as opting out, leaving the retiree in traditional Medicare with the employer continuing to pay for it.

Amends the Medicare Advantage waiver rules so the Health and Human Services Secretary may no longer waive the requirement that an individual affirmatively elect to enroll in an employer group Medicare Advantage plan before being enrolled.
States the sense of Congress that seniors have the right to choose between traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that currently move retirees into Medicare Advantage automatically, and the private insurers running those employer group plans. If non-response keeps a retiree in traditional Medicare, the employer must continue paying for traditional Medicare coverage instead of the usually cheaper private plan, and insurers receive fewer members enrolled without a signed choice.

drawbacks.text: The bill treats silence as opting out, which means an employer must keep paying for traditional Medicare coverage for retirees who never respond. Employers that save money by moving retirees into often-lower-cost Medicare Advantage plans would bear that cost, which could affect the benefits or premiums they offer other workers.

Medicare Advantage plans often include extra benefits or lower out-of-pocket costs, and automatic enrollment has moved many retirees into those plans. Requiring affirmative opt-in could leave some retirees in traditional Medicare who would have been better off in a private plan and never got around to choosing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and narrow: it protects people with employer retiree coverage from being enrolled in a private plan without ever saying yes, and keeps a default of traditional Medicare. The cost falls on employers, who must keep funding traditional Medicare coverage for non-responders, and on insurers, who lose passively enrolled members. It is a consumer-choice protection, not a broad health coverage change; it does not touch the large majority of Medicare beneficiaries who have no employer group plan.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and then to the Health subcommittee, but neither committee ever took it up and it never reached the House floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Ritchie Torres introduced the bill on September 14, 2023, joined by Representative Nicole Malliotakis as an original cosponsor, making the bill bipartisan from the start.
The Speaker referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, splitting jurisdiction between the two panels that oversee Medicare.
It was referred to the Health subcommittees in September 2023 and again in December 2024, the only actions taken in its fifteen months on the books.

No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill under the rule that legislation does not carry over between Congresses.
It ended with three cosponsors: two of 224 House Republicans and one of 216 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with retiree group plans and the Medicare Advantage insurers that run them, who keep enrolling retirees without an affirmative choice and avoid a rule requiring continued payment for traditional Medicare. Retirees who wanted the protection are left with the status quo.

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as guaranteeing seniors a choice between traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage.

for.name: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor at introduction, making the bill bipartisan.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee that received the bill never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, so it sat without action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee's Health subcommittee took a routine referral in September 2023 and again in December 2024 but the committee never advanced the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan by design, with a Democratic sponsor and two Republican cosponsors, and no one voted on it or publicly against it; it simply never advanced, so no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.note: Employer group Medicare Advantage plans gain members from automatic enrollment of retirees who may not read or respond to enrollment notices. The bill requires an affirmative choice before enrollment and treats silence as staying in traditional Medicare, removing that stream of passively enrolled members. Their interest in keeping the auto-enrollment default runs against retirees' choice.

The bill bans employers from involuntarily moving seniors into Medicare Advantage and requires them to keep paying for traditional Medicare coverage when a retiree does not opt in. Employers that shift retirees to private plans to cut retiree health costs would face continued traditional Medicare obligations, though the rule also gives them a clear consent standard.
